metadata.title: The future of intelligence: A prediction of the FLynn effect based on past student assessment studies until the year 2100

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study does not analyze individual-level microdata from TIMSS/PISA/PIRLS; instead, it aggregates international student achievement results across countries and measurement years (1995–2019) and then converts study means to a common IQ-scale. Because the analysis is performed at the country/region level using published international report statistics (and not a student-level dataset), standard ILSA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) are not described or applied. The paper also does not report any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife), consistent with its use of deterministic transformations (scale conversions, averaging of differences) and country-specific regression coefficients. Preprocessing includes excluding countries with insufficient measurement points (fewer than five) and applying an outlier correction based on plausibility thresholds before averaging model-based predictions.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variable is not an ILSA cognitive achievement score at the student level; instead, the authors use published country-level mean achievement results from TIMSS/PISA/PIRLS and convert them to an IQ-scale. Missing-data handling for student-level nonresponse/PV generation is therefore not part of the analysis pipeline described in the paper. The paper does, however, apply inclusion rules at the country level (minimum number of measurement points) and excludes countries with insufficient data, which is a different mechanism than PV-based missingness handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors compile international achievement results from TIMSS (1995–2019; treated separately for TIMSS 4th and 8th grades), PISA (2000–2018; reading, mathematics, science; plus problem solving in 2003), and PIRLS (2001–2016; 4th graders in reading). They apply corrections to published scores for school attendance/age comparability and then require at least five measurement points per country to be included in the longitudinal development analyses. The full set of 104 countries with results is reduced to 79 countries after applying the minimum-measurement criterion. Countries with too few measurement points (e.g., Belarus, Belize, Brunei, El Salvador, Honduras, Mauritius, Mongolia, Pakistan, Venezuela) and large countries with insufficient waves (e.g., China and India) are excluded from the final 79-country sample used for regression-based forecasting.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict predicts societal cognitive development (expressed as IQ on a Greenwich-IQ scal, finding that This paper predicts societal cognitive development (expressed as IQ on a Greenwich-IQ scale) up to 2100 by using past international student achievement results from TIMSS (1995–2019; grades 4 and 8; mathematics and science), PISA (2000–2018; reading, mathematics, science), and PIRLS (2001–2016; reading). The authors convert published study means to a common IQ scale, compute decadal gains via trend subtraction, and estimate country-specific linear (y=a+bx) and nonlinear quadratic (y=a+bx+cx²) regressions using up to 14 measurement years (1995–2019) where available. Across 79 countries, the worldwide corrected mean IQ increases from 91.29 (2020) to 93.51 (2030), 95.69 (2050), and 101.25 (2100), with an average decadal gain of 1.25 IQ points. Model choice strongly affects extremity: nonlinear predictions yield much larger dispersion (uncorrected SD 229.78 vs corrected SD 95.43), and outlier correction substantially reduces implausible values. Limitations include the absence of student-level ML modeling, no PV-based uncertainty quantification, and reliance on extrapolation assumptions that the authors themselves flag as likely to fail over long horizons. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses statistical regression and trend extrapolation, it does not train or evaluate machine learning algorithms on student-level ILSA microdata, and it does not report PV-based achievement modeling. Consequently, fields required for predictive ML extraction (e.g., ml_techniques and main_findings structured by target-variable prediction performance) are not applicable. The analysis is primarily a country-level statistical forecasting exercise using aggregated international assessment results, so there are no ML target variables, top predictors, or ML performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) to map into the ML schema.
